questions: Can the subgraph be any subset of vertices and edges of T, or must it be an induced subgraph (i.e., must include all edges of T between the chosen vertices)?
When selecting a subgraph, are isolated vertices (degree 0) allowed, or must every selected vertex have degree exactly 1 or 4 within the subgraph?
Must the subgraph itself be connected, or is a forest of multiple tree components each satisfying the degree condition acceptable?

If the subgraph is required to be a tree, does it need to be a spanning tree of its vertex set (i.e., contain exactly |V|-1 edges), or can extra edges be omitted as long as the degree condition holds?
Are vertices of degree 4 in the subgraph required to have exactly four incident edges within the subgraph, or can they have fewer as long as the overall degree condition is met?
Should the answer be -1 only when no subgraph with at least one vertex satisfies the conditions, or also when the only possible subgraphs have fewer than some minimum size?
Is there any requirement on the labeling or ordering of vertices in the output, or is only the size of the largest alkane subgraph needed?
Are multiple edges or self‑loops possible in the input tree, and if so, how should they be treated when forming a subgraph?
answers: Not specified beyond what's given; assume the subgraph must be induced, i.e. contain all edges of T between the selected vertices.
Not specified beyond what's given; every selected vertex must have degree exactly 1 or 4 within the subgraph, so isolated vertices are not allowed.
Not specified beyond what's given; assume the subgraph must remain a single connected tree, per the alkane definition (an undirected tree).
Yes, as a tree, the subgraph must have exactly |V|-1 edges; extra edges cannot be omitted while keeping it a tree.
Not specified beyond what's given; a degree-4 vertex's four incident edges are counted within the subgraph itself, not the original tree.
The output should be -1 whenever no valid alkane subgraph -- one containing at least one degree-4 vertex -- exists.
Not specified beyond what's given; only the size of the largest alkane subgraph is needed.
Not applicable in the strict sense since the input is guaranteed to be a tree (no self-loops/multi-edges), but any chosen subgraph must still satisfy the stated degree conditions.
inline_prompts: You are given an undirected tree T with N vertices, numbered 1, 2, \ldots, N. The i-th edge is an undirected edge connecting vertices A_i and B_i. A graph is defined to be an alkane if and only if it satisfies the following conditions: - The graph is an undirected tree. - Every vertex has degree 1 or 4. Determine whether there exists a subgraph of T that is an alkane, and if so, find the maximum number of vertices in such a subgraph. Input The input is given from Standard Input in the following format: N A_1 B_1 A_2 B_2 \vdots A_{N - 1} B_{N - 1} Output If there exists a subgraph of T that is an alkane, print the maximum number of vertices in such a subgraph. Otherwise, print -1. Constraints - 1 \leq N \leq 2 \times 10^5 - 1 \leq A_i, B_i \leq N - All input values are integers.
